When Tenzin was nine, his parents lit up only when a test came home with a big number. His father Yogesh would say, "Ninety-eight! Show everyone." When a paper came home with a lower score, Yogesh went quiet and turned the television up. Tenzin began to slip the weaker papers into the bottom of his bag.

By fifteen, his teacher Zubin held up Tenzin's notebook in class. "Look at this. Not a single crossing-out." The whole class clapped, and Tenzin felt warm and safe. He started rewriting whole pages when he made one blot, staying up until midnight, because a flawed page felt like a way of losing that clapping. On the day of a class test he scored lower than usual, went pale and told nobody.

At dinner Yogesh asked how school had gone and Tenzin said, "Fine." The fear stayed under the word.

qa.q: What did Zubin hold up in front of the class when Tenzin was fifteen?
qa.a: Zubin held up Tenzin's notebook and pointed out that it had no crossing-out.

qa.q: How does the way Yogesh responds at home connect to Tenzin's rewriting of pages at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine Tenzin learns that his parents light up for big numbers and go quiet otherwise, so he hides weak papers; at fifteen the praise for flawless work makes being perfect feel like the price of safety, so he rewrites pages and hides a poor test.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he said school was fine at dinner?
qa.a: Tenzin was afraid and ashamed of the lower score, hiding it because it might cost him the warmth he gets for being flawless.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to make Tenzin feel safe about mistakes?
qa.a: Yogesh could respond warmly to weaker papers too, asking what Tenzin learned, so that love does not depend on the number.

grounding: Perfectionism from a parent who responds only to marks to a teenager who learns that praise and safety come with flawless work, hiding the fear underneath.

passage:
Five-year-old Suraj stood in the middle of a floor covered with toy cars and picture books. His father Naveen was tired and said, "Tidy up, please." Suraj folded his arms. Then he said, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story." Naveen laughed. "Deal." Ten minutes later, the room was clear, and they were on the sofa with a story.

In the next room, Suraj's older sister Chaitanya was on the phone. On Monday she had said that her friend was the most loyal person alive. On Friday, after the friend forgot to save her a seat at lunch, she said, "She is a total traitor. I'm done with her forever." Naveen, passing the door, said only, "Sounds like you're really hurt." Chaitanya sighed. "She did forget the seat. But she also stayed with me all week when I was sick."

Her voice lowered as she said it.

qa.q: What deal did Suraj offer his father about tidying up?
qa.a: Suraj offered, "I do the cars, you do the books, then we read a story."

qa.q: How does the way Suraj divides the tidying differ from the way Chaitanya divides her view of her friend?
qa.a: Suraj splits the tidying into cars and books so that each of them does a part; Chaitanya calls her friend the most loyal person alive on Monday and a total traitor on Friday, then admits the friend also stayed with her all week. One is a fair split of work, the other is splitting a person into all good or all bad.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when she called her friend a traitor?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt hurt and let down by the forgotten seat, and the strong feeling made it hard to hold the friend's kindness in mind.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that helped Chaitanya?
qa.a: Naveen named her hurt instead of arguing about the friend, which gave Chaitanya room to remember the good part.

grounding: A contrast between two different kinds of splitting in one household: a child dividing a chore fairly, and a teenager splitting a friend into all good or all bad.

Ten minutes into a rainy Sunday, five-year-old Tejas flopped on the sofa. "I'm bored. What can I do? Can I have the tablet?" His father Vikas looked up from the newspaper. He did not hand over the tablet, and he did not offer a list of ideas. He put a large cardboard box, a roll of tape and a marker on the floor. "Here," he said, and went back to reading. Tejas sighed and complained for a minute. Then he cut a hole in the side and announced, "It's a bus."

At ten, in the long heat of a summer afternoon with no screens, Tejas draped bedsheets over two chairs and the bookcase. He built a fort with a secret entrance, drew a map of his kingdom and invented a card game with his cousin Saurabh that filled hours. When his father called for tea, Tejas said, "Five more minutes." He had not looked at the clock once.

qa.q: What did Vikas put on the floor when Tejas said he was bored?
qa.a: Vikas put down a large cardboard box, a roll of tape and a marker.

qa.q: How does Tejas's boredom at five lead to his afternoon at ten?
qa.a: At five he feels the discomfort of boredom and asks for a screen, but simple materials and time turn it into a bus; by ten the same boredom, left alone, becomes a fort, a map and a card game, showing that tolerated boredom grows self-directed interest.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he flopped on the sofa and asked for the tablet?
qa.a: Tejas felt restless and uncomfortable, wanting the easy relief of a screen.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that helped Tejas at five?
qa.a: Vikas gave simple materials without solving the boredom for Tejas, so the boy could invent something himself.

grounding: Boredom as the doorway to invention: a child restless for a screen at five, and the same child building his own world at ten when boredom is tolerated.

At five, Manjula clapped a hand over her mouth and shrieked with giggles whenever her father Arnab made his moustache wiggle and called the cat "Mister Cow." She tried the wrong words herself: "Papa, the spoon is a shoe!" They laughed until the tea went cold, leaning into each other.

At nine, Manjula stood up to read a paragraph aloud and tripped over "temperature". A titter rose. Her ears burned. Then she crossed her eyes, blew out her cheeks and said, "Tempra-tricycle!" The class roared, and Manjula bowed. She looked in charge of the moment. Later, though, she went very quiet at her desk, tearing at the edge of her notebook.

Her teacher Farida noticed and, after class, said gently, "That was a funny rescue. Reading aloud can feel scary, can't it? Shall we practise the hard words together?" Manjula nodded slowly and let out a shaky breath.

qa.q: What word did Manjula trip over when reading aloud at nine?
qa.a: Manjula tripped over the word "temperature".

qa.q: How does the humour Manjula uses at five differ from the humour she uses at nine?
qa.a: At five Manjula giggles with Arnab over wrong words and funny faces; at nine she crosses her eyes and says "Tempra-tricycle" so the class roars after she trips, then goes quiet at her desk. The first is shared play, the second is a joke that keeps control of the moment and hides worry.

qa.q: What was Manjula probably feeling when she tore at the edge of her notebook after class?
qa.a: Manjula was embarrassed and worried underneath the jokes, and her torn notebook edge showed the nervousness she had covered with clowning.

qa.q: What did Farida do that helped Manjula?
qa.a: Farida praised the funny rescue, named that reading aloud can feel scary, and offered to practise the hard words together.

grounding: Humour used two ways: a young child's silly-sounds play that builds closeness, and a school-age child's clowning to cover embarrassment.

On Thursday, Dhruv told his mother Disha that his science project would take ten minutes and he would begin after dinner on Friday. "It's only a chart," he said. On Friday night he found he had to cut out pictures, look up three facts and colour the border. At half past nine he was still gluing, and the chart had gone crooked.

Earlier that week, Dhruv had promised his father Uday, "I'll draw the mango in five minutes, then we can go to the park." Uday looked at the clock. An hour later Dhruv was still shading the leaves, absorbed and surprised. "Is it evening already?" he asked. He had not been trying to fool anyone. He truly thought five minutes was enough.

On Saturday, Uday sat with him and wrote next to each task how long the last one had taken. Dhruv stared at the list and said, "Oh. It's not ten minutes, it's more like an hour."

qa.q: How long did Dhruv say his science project would take?
qa.a: Dhruv said the project would take ten minutes.

qa.q: What do the science chart and the mango drawing have in common?
qa.a: In both Dhruv gives a short time, ten minutes for the chart and five for the mango, and then finds it takes far longer, because he pictures the ideal path and has little sense of how long things take, so his promises are sincere but unreliable.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he asked whether it was evening already?
qa.a: Dhruv felt surprised and absorbed, honestly unaware that an hour had gone.

qa.q: What could Uday do to help Dhruv plan time better?
qa.a: Uday could do what he did, writing down how long each task really took, so Dhruv can compare guesses with real times.

grounding: The planning fallacy in a child: promising short times for a project and a drawing and being surprised by how much longer they take.

passage:
At sixteen, Devika had a history project due in three weeks, and she opened the file every evening and closed it again. If she started, she might discover she could not do it well. So she reorganised her shelves, watched two episodes of a show and told herself, "I work better under pressure." Her teacher Samir asked how it was going. "Fine," she said.

Four years later, in college, a paper was due at nine the next morning. At six in the evening Devika began, and fear turned to energy. She wrote through the night with coffee and her friend Rafiq's notes, and submitted at dawn. The grade was decent. "See?" she said to Rafiq, bleary-eyed. "Last minute works."

Two days later she caught a cold from exhaustion and missed the next class. She noticed, without saying it aloud, that she had got a lower mark than Rafiq, who had started a week early and had gone out to dinner the night before.

qa.q: At what time on the deadline day did Devika begin her college paper?
qa.a: Devika began at six in the evening.

qa.q: How are the delay at sixteen and the all-night sprint at twenty connected?
qa.a: At sixteen Devika avoids starting because a poor result would expose weakness, and at twenty the same delay ends in a panic sprint that works well enough to teach her that last minute is fine, although the cost is exhaustion and a lower mark than Rafiq.

qa.q: What was Devika probably feeling as she opened and closed the file every evening at sixteen?
qa.a: Devika was afraid of doing badly, so she protected her self-image by not starting.

qa.q: What could Devika try before the next deadline?
qa.a: She could start with a small, rough section early and ask for feedback, so fear of a poor result does not keep her waiting for panic.

grounding: Procrastination linked across ages: a teenager avoiding a project to protect her self-image, and the later panic sprint that seems to work but carries a cost.
